questions.q: What is the key difference between polling and event-driven processing?
options: Polling repeatedly checks a source on a timer; event-driven processing has the source announce events that directly invoke the consumer
Polling is always faster than event-driven processing
Event-driven processing requires a dedicated EC2 instance to run
They are two names for the same pattern
questions.explain: Polling costs compute and adds latency even when nothing changed; event-driven processing reacts only when an actual event occurs.

questions.q: Which AWS service lets a fast producer hand work to a slower consumer without either one polling the other?
options: SQS (Simple Queue Service)
IAM
CloudWatch Logs
Route 53
questions.explain: SQS queues messages so a producer can move on immediately while a consumer, like a Lambda function, processes them as they arrive.

questions.q: Which event source is used for cron-like scheduled Lambda invocations, e.g. running a function every night at 2 AM?
options: EventBridge scheduled rules
S3 PUT events
DynamoDB Streams
IAM policies
questions.explain: EventBridge scheduled rules invoke a function on a timer, still push-based rather than the function itself polling a clock.

options: A feed of change events (inserts, updates, deletes) from a DynamoDB table that can trigger a function
A way to run SQL queries against DynamoDB
A backup mechanism for DynamoDB tables
A queue for batching S3 uploads
questions.explain: DynamoDB Streams emits change records that Lambda can subscribe to and react to in near real time.

questions.q: According to this lesson, why does event-driven design keep components 'decoupled'?
options: The event source just publishes an event without knowing or caring what's subscribed to it
Because it requires all consumers to share the same IAM role
Because polling scripts must be manually linked to each consumer
Decoupling is not a property of event-driven design
questions.explain: A producer like S3 doesn't need to know a Lambda function exists — it just emits events, and any current or future subscriber can react.
